# TUI — Tables

### Rule 106 : Table standardization

- Use `theme.DefaultTableStyles()` for all tables
- Bold headers with ColorSecondary (see Rule 118)
- Selected row with ColorHighlight
- Consistent borders

### Rule 116 : the rendered row occupies exactly the inside of the viewport

**The selected row must extend all the way to the viewport's right border.**

The calculation belongs to `internal/ui/datatable`, and to it alone. A view
passes the **full viewport width, borders included** — `Resize` strips out
the borders and the padding `bubbles/table` adds per cell (`Padding(0, 1)`,
i.e. +2 per rendered column).

```go
func (m *Model) resize(width, height int) {
    m.table.Resize(width, max(height-1, 1)) // no -2, no max(…, 20)
}
```

Subtracting the borders a second time is the rule's most discreet defect:
the table is then correct at *every* width and also ends two cells too soon
at every one of them. A local floor (`max(…, 20)`) is the mirror-image
mistake — it makes the table wider than the viewport when the terminal is
narrow, which is exactly the forbidden overflow.

#### The invariant is stated over the **rendered** extent

```go
// ✅ CORRECT
if got, want := m.table.RenderedWidth(), width-2; got != want { … }

// ❌ WRONG — wrong as soon as a column is dropped
total := 0
for _, col := range m.table.Table().Columns() { total += col.Width }
if want := width - 2 - len(cols)*2; total != want { … }
```

A column dropped for lack of room renders nothing — no header, no cell, no
padding — and its two cells go back into the budget. The sum of the declared
columns plus two each therefore asks for less than what the row occupies,
and fails on an otherwise correct layout. This is D61 seen from the other
side.

#### Which width library measures what

Lip Gloss v2 and the viewport measure with `x/ansi` (`ansi.StringWidth`,
grapheme clusters); `datatable` pads and truncates with `go-runewidth` (render.go).
Rule 116 holds only while the two agree on what a cell holds.
`TestDatatableWidthAgreesWithTheGraphemeWidth` pins the agreement for flags, ZWJ
sequences, Nerd Font glyphs, CJK and combining marks. **Known divergence:** a
VS16 emoji (`❤️`, `✔️`) is 1 cell for `runewidth` and 2 for `x/ansi`;
`REDACTED` pins it, and the width tests leave such
glyphs out. Whether the terminal draws 1 or 2 cells depends on mode 2027. Do not
put a VS16 emoji in a table cell. A library fix will fail that test, which is
the cue to turn it into an agreement test.

#### Every column declares its nature (§3.45)

`Sizing` has **no** default value: `SizingFixed` (exact width) or
`SizingContent` (content width, floored at `MinWidth`, capped at
`MaxWidth`). `TestEveryColumnDeclaresItsSizing` scans the sources and fails,
naming the file, line, and column.

`MinWidth` is a **floor**, not a request. What gives way beyond that is an
**entire** column: `Optional` ones first, rightmost first, then the others
if needed. The exception is an `Optional` column marked `YieldsToContent`: it
is removed, in drop order, before a required content column is cut below its
widest value (the order does not change, only the moment; DEVDESK-128). Fewer
correct columns beat all of them being wrong — truncating a
count column would render `142` as `14…`, and nothing on screen tells the
two apart.

Forbidden:
- ❌ Computing column widths inside a view
- ❌ Subtracting the borders before `Resize`, or clamping the width passed in
- ❌ Checking Rule 116 by summing the declared columns
- ❌ Leaving a column without a `Sizing`
- ❌ `Background()` on `s.Cell` (masks `s.Selected.Background()`)

### Rule 122 : `Cell` measures, `Style` colors — never the reverse ⚠️

**`Cell` returns plain text, with no ANSI sequence. Color goes through
`Style`, and through nothing else.**

**Why.** A cell is measured and truncated *before* it is dressed up, and the
measurement goes through `runewidth`, which counts an escape sequence's
bytes as width. A string of 7 visible cells carrying a color measures 28: it
therefore gets truncated in a column that is twice wide enough, and the cut
falls *inside* the escape sequence — `"\x1b[38;2;166;2…"`. The unterminated
sequence then bleeds onto every following row.

This is a limitation of `bubbles/table`, not of Bubble Tea or lipgloss, and
it is the same in Bubbles v2 (`charm.land/bubbles/v2`). `internal/ui/datatable` therefore
renders its own rows (`render.go`): the text is measured while still plain,
color is applied afterward. **The prohibition therefore targets `Cell`, not
color.**

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the text is measurable, the color is decided separately
{
    Title: "Severity", MinWidth: 10,
    Cell:  func(f scan.Finding) string { return string(f.Severity) },
    Style: func(f scan.Finding) lipgloss.Style {
        return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity))
    },
}

// ❌ WRONG — color becomes part of what gets measured
{
    Cell: func(f scan.Finding) string {
        return theme.SeverityTextStyle(string(f.Severity)).Render(string(f.Severity))
    },
}
```

#### Two colors in one cell — `Cut` and `TailStyle`

**A cell can have two runs instead of one, and the measure-first order still
holds.** `Column.Cut(item) int` and `Column.TailStyle(item) lipgloss.Style`
exist for two callers — the containers load gauges (§3.71) and the `ws` Git
Status cell, whose branch keeps the text color while its markers warn
(§3.94) — so `Style` colors the first `Cut(item)` cells of the text and
`TailStyle` colors the rest. Every character either caller puts in such a cell
is single-width: `Cut` is a rune index, and a double-width glyph would move the
boundary. This is not the gradient the top of this rule forbids: `Cut` reads the
*already-fitted* plain text, after truncation and padding, at the exact point
`Style` already colors from — nothing styled is ever measured, it is the same
order applied to two runs. Nil on both (every column but the two gauges and
Git Status) keeps the one-run path.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — two colors, both decided after Cell's text is final
{
    Title: "1 core", Sizing: SizingFixed, MinWidth: theme.GaugeWidth,
    Cell:      func(c docker.Container) string { return theme.Gauge(theme.GaugeWidth) },
    Style:     func(c docker.Container) lipgloss.Style { return theme.LoadTextStyle(c.CPUPercent) },
    Cut:       func(c docker.Container) int { return theme.GaugeFillWidth(c.CPUPercent, theme.GaugeWidth) },
    TailStyle: func(c docker.Container) lipgloss.Style { return theme.GaugeTrackStyle() },
}
```

Dropped only on a row a view has coloured whole (below) — error, busy, a CVE
severity — for the same reason `Style` is: a color that ends before the row
does would still close that solid highlight mid-row. On the plain "normal"
selection both runs *are* consulted, the same as `Style` is there.

#### N colored runs — `Spans`

`Column.Spans(item) []Span` generalises the two-run split to any number of
runs: `Span{Width, Style}` paints `Width` cells of the *finished* text, left to
right, and the cells left after the last span take `Style`. Same order as
`Cut`: the text is measured, truncated and padded first, then colored. A
negative width counts as 0, a zero width renders nothing (no empty ANSI
sequence), a span past the end of the cell is cut. Widths are rune counts, so
the cell holds single-width glyphs. A nil or empty result takes the ordinary
one-run path, byte for byte. **`Spans` takes precedence over `Cut`/`TailStyle`,
and a column declaring both is rejected** (`TestNoColumnDeclaresSpansWithCutOrTailStyle`).
Like `Cut`, spans are dropped on a row a view has coloured whole (error, busy,
severity) and repainted on `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold on the plain
"normal" selection.

#### Selected row

**`Style` is not consulted for a row a view has coloured whole** — error,
busy, a CVE severity, via `SelectedStyles` or the busy override. It is
handed to `styles.Selected` instead, and a color inside it closes with a
reset that carries away that solid background for the rest of the row: the
highlight would stop halfway through. That row answers "what state is this
in," and no column color is worth losing it.

**The plain "normal" selection is the exception (§3.72).**
`Style` *is* consulted there — `cellStyle` composites it with
`ColorTableLineSelected` and bold **on every cell itself**, rather than
dropping it for one outer wrap. That sidesteps the defect above instead of
reproducing it: a cell's own reset only ever uncovers the *same* background
the next cell immediately repaints, so nothing but that background is ever
exposed between two cells. `Cut`/`TailStyle` follow the same rule: both runs
repaint `ColorTableLineSelected` and bold themselves (`runStyle`'s
`selected` branch), so a reset between the two runs never uncovers anything
but that shared background either — a load gauge keeps its fill/track split
under the cursor instead of collapsing to `Style`'s single fill colour. The
track becomes a visible rail rather than an invisible one: its own colour
(`ColorSeverityLow`) and the selection background (`ColorTableLineSelected`)
are two distinct keys, not one aliased to the other.

#### Background

lipgloss does not inherit a background (Rule 115), and the viewport's style
only covers cells that emit nothing. `render.go` therefore gives an explicit
background to **every** cell of an unselected row, colored or not —
otherwise a single colored cell would strip the background off everything
that follows it. A column that declares only a `Foreground` automatically
receives `ColorBackground`.

#### Color discipline

A color that appears everywhere tells you nothing:

- a counter at `0`, a `-`, a missing value → `theme.DimStyle`;
- the nominal, majority state (a `running` container) → the default text
  color, **not** green;
- color is reserved for what deserves to be spotted without reading.

**The exception, and what defines it: a column where the absence of color
is already taken.** The `CI` column has three absences — never scanned, not
gradable, score withheld — and all three render in `DimStyle`. An `A` in
ordinary text color is distinguishable from a grey `-` only by a shade,
across four cells. Green there separates **a grade from an absence**, not
two nominal values from each other: that is exactly what the rule above
forbids elsewhere, and exactly what it requires here. That is the
criterion, and not "it's important" — if a column's absences were already
distinguishable, green would go back to being noise.

**The second and third declared exceptions: the containers load gauges
(§3.71).** Every cell of a gauge is the *same* glyph (`░`) — filled and empty
alike — so unlike every other colored column in this application, color here
is not a spotlight on top of text that already says something. It is the
**only** thing that says anything at all: with one glyph, a cell reads as
filled or empty exclusively by which color it carries.

- The *fill* is green below 75%, orange, then red, on Rule 128's ground:
  one alphabet of severity across the application, so a nearly-full gauge
  reads like a CRITICAL finding without reading the number beside it.
- The *track* — `theme.GaugeTrackStyle()`, aliasing `ColorSeverityLow` — is
  fixed, whatever the fill's own level is. Without it, an idle row's `░` and
  a critical row's `░` would carry whatever color `Style` had picked for
  that row's *fill*, which would read as the level bleeding into cells that
  were never filled. `ColorSeverityLow` defaults to the same tone as
  `ColorDim` (the counter zeroes above): the rail reads as unremarkable for
  the same reason a `0` does, which is the argument this bullet already
  makes generalised to a bar instead of a digit.

This is close to the CI column's own criterion (an idle gauge, entirely
track-colored, *is* what "no load" looks like) but reaches further: the CI
column's colors sit on top of letters that already read on their own; a
gauge's don't. Removing the color here does not fall back to plain text
that still says something — it falls back to a row of identical `░`.
Accepted cost, stated rather than discovered: most containers idle near zero,
so most rows carry a short green sliver in a track-colored field, both present
at once (`Cut`/`TailStyle`, above).

**The fourth declared exception: the Sig column's proven signature (§3.82).**
`internal/ui/sigcol` renders a Verified image's `IconOK` in green, while the
Update column (`theme.UpdateStyle`) renders its "up to date" `IconOK` dim. The
same glyph, two colors — and the reason is **not** the CI column's: in both
columns the glyphs already tell every state apart, so the shade is not what
separates the check mark from the `-`. The criterion is what the state *is*:

| | Update — "up to date" | Sig — Verified |
|---|---|---|
| How common | the majority, the resting state | rare: only images a rule covers, and only once proven |
| What it says | nothing happened, nothing to do | a guarantee was established for this digest |
| Its counterpart | a blue "update available" — the action | a red cross — the refusal |

Up to date is the nominal state this rule keeps out of color, exactly like a
`running` container. Verified is the positive half of a security verdict whose
negative half is red: dimming it would leave the column able to say only that
something is wrong, never that something was proven. That is the test for a
further exception of this kind, and not "it is good news": **a rare, established guarantee
whose absence or failure is itself colored**. A state that is merely the
common, fine case stays dim.

**The fifth declared exception: the token breakdown bars (DEVDESK-98).** A
`Spans` cell made of one repeated glyph, where color is the only way to tell
the parts of the bar apart. The criterion, and not "a bar looks nicer": the
cell repeats a single glyph so color is the only separator between its parts,
**and** the exact figures are readable without color on the same screen or one
key away (the numeric columns, the breakdown view). The colors name
**categories** (`theme.TokenStyle` roles: input, output, cache read, cache
write), never severity or gauge colors: a red part of a bar must not read as
"critical", nor a green one as "healthy". A bar whose figures are available
nowhere without color does not qualify. Accepted cost, stated rather than
discovered: without color the bar only says "has tokens"; the exact figures stay
readable elsewhere.

Checklist:
- [ ] No `style.Render(...)` inside what `Cell` returns
- [ ] Status icons as plain text: `theme.IconError + " error"`
- [ ] Spinners as plain text: `frame + " scanning"`
- [ ] Per-cell color via `Style`, never via `Cell`
- [ ] Multi-run cells via Cut/TailStyle or Spans, never by styling inside Cell
- [ ] Selected-row color via `SelectedStyles` / `TableStylesForState/Severity()`
- [ ] Zeros and placeholders are `DimStyle`, not colored

### Rule 125 : Icon column alignment

> A row-level state (running, queued, failed, ...) is the activity column
> below, and `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` enforces it (A-16,
> DEVDESK-143).

**Any icon column (or icon + short text) must be left-aligned.**

Nerd Font icons have variable width depending on the terminal. Left alignment is the only one that guarantees consistent rendering.

| Content type | Alignment |
|-----------------|------------|
| Icon alone | **Left** |
| Icon + short text | **Left** |
| Alphanumeric text | Left (default) |

#### An icon in the first column **is** a column

When a `datatable`'s first column carries a glyph, it is a column in its own
right — not a prefix stuck onto the neighboring text cell.

| | |
|---|---|
| Title | **empty**. The glyph reads in a glance; a header would be naming something that does not need naming, and `eza` does not put one there either. |
| Width | `datatable.IconColumnWidth` (2): the glyph, plus one cell so it does not touch the text. Two, not one — a Nerd Font glyph renders double-width on some terminals, and a single cell would truncate it there. |
| `Sizing` | `SizingFixed`. Nothing to measure. |
| `Less` / `Search` | **none**. It adds no text anyone could type, so filtering stays on the name columns; and a comparator would cost two more cells to fit its sort arrow. |

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the glyph has its own column
{
    Title: "", Sizing: datatable.SizingFixed, MinWidth: datatable.IconColumnWidth,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return r.icon() },
},
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 16,
    Cell:   func(r row) string { return r.Name },
    Search: func(r row) string { return r.Name },
},

// ❌ WRONG — the glyph stuck into the identifying column
{
    Title: "Name", Sizing: datatable.SizingContent, MinWidth: 18,
    Cell: func(r row) string { return theme.IconDocker + " " + r.Name },
},
```

**What sticking it in costs**, and this is what settles it: the identifying
column spends its width on something that is not the name, and a
`SizingContent` then measures the glyph along with it — so the table's most
contested column reserves two cells for an icon, at every width.

#### An icon's color goes through a **role**, never through the glyph

Rule 122 applies here as everywhere: `Cell` renders the bare glyph, `Style`
colors it. What Rule 125 adds is **where the color comes from** —
`theme.IconStyle(role)`, and a role declared in `theme/iconcolors.go`.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the view names a meaning, the theme answers with a color
Cell:  func(r row) string { return nodeKindIcon(r.node) },
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style { return theme.IconStyle(nodeKindRole(r.node)) },

// ❌ WRONG — the view decides the hue
Style: func(r row) lipgloss.Style {
    return lipgloss.NewStyle().Foreground(theme.ColorSecondary)
},
```

**A codepoint is not a name.** A table of `U+F0849 → ColorSecondary` cannot
be reviewed: nothing on the line says whether the entry is correct, so an
error there is indistinguishable from a deliberate choice. A role can be
discussed, which is why it is the key.

The roles are overridable via a theme file (`icon_namespace`,
`icon_repository`, `icon_vis_*`, `icon_image`, `icon_container`; `IconRoleContainer`
is the resting icon of a running container, `ColorText` by default) — unlike syntax colors, which are closed
aliases: an icon is the first thing seen on a row, so it is the part of the
palette a user is most likely to have an opinion about.

**All three icon tables declare a `Style`** — `ws`, `:sec`, and the
explorer — and a fourth that did not declare one would be the application's
only monochrome icon column. A missing role shows: the cell falls back to
`ColorText` (see `IconColor`), so an oversight renders ordinary text rather
than nothing.

**The same object keeps its color from one view to another.** A git repo is
`IconRoleRepository` in `ws`, in `:sec`, and in the explorer — the role is
shared, not duplicated. This is the property for which the key is a meaning
rather than a glyph: the three views do not even show the same glyph for it.

**The granularity is that of the action, not that of the type.** `ws`
colors in three classes — repo, directory, file — which are exactly the
three branches of `availability.go`, and **not** a shade per language the
way `eza` does: `.go` versus `.rs` changes no shortcut on the row, so the
color would say nothing. An icon column is colored by what the row lets you
do.

**The color disappears under the cursor**, like that of any colored column:
the selected row is rendered whole by `styles.Selected` (Rule 122). An icon
column therefore cannot be the *only* carrier of a piece of information —
which is why the explorer's kind stays readable another way (the glyph
outside selection, the position in the tree inside it).

The three tables concerned are `ws`, `containers`, and the `:sec` inventory,
and they declare the same constant. `TestAnIconColumnIsUntitledAndTwoCellsWide`
(`internal/ui/datatable`) scans the sources and rejects a titleless column
that invents its own width. It does not see the other half — a glyph stuck
into a text cell is indistinguishable from a name that starts with a
glyph — which stays a matter for review.

#### The activity column

**In a view with long-running operations (jobs, agents, containers), the first
column is the activity indicator.** It is built by `datatable.IndicatorColumn`,
never by a literal `Column` with an `Indicator` field set (`TestOnlyIndicatorColumnSetsIndicator`
rejects it). It keeps the icon-column shape above: untitled, `SizingFixed`,
`datatable.IconColumnWidth`. When the row is at rest (`indicator.Idle`) the
cell shows the row's own icon via its `theme.IconStyle` role, or an empty cell.

- **The color says the state, never the operation.** A scan, a clone and a
  `docker stop` that are running all look the same: `●` / `○`. What is being
  done is the footer's and the Jobs view's business.
- **No green for "done".** `Done` is `◉` in `ColorActivityNeutral`. Green stays
  reserved for the exceptions Rule 122 lists.
- **The colors are closed aliases**, assigned in `ApplyTheme`:
  `ColorActivityRunning`, `ColorActivityNeutral`, `ColorActivitySuspended`,
  `ColorActivityFailed`. They are not `icon_*` roles and no theme file gains a
  key: a theme that retuned them per state would break the one alphabet of
  states the application shares.
- **The glyph carries the meaning, the color repeats it.** Under the cursor
  the color is repainted on `ColorTableLineSelected` and the glyph still reads.
- **The blink phase is read at render.** The router's `jobs.FrameMsg` carries
  it; the view calls `m.table.SetBlinkPhase(msg.Blink)` and nothing is rebuilt.
  Without the call the phase is on: a running row shows a steady `●`. A view
  starts no timer of its own for a row (`app.motion: static` pins it on).
- **Guarded.** `internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` (A-16, DEVDESK-143) fails
  a view whose table is neither on the activity column nor declared exempt, and
  a migrated package that holds `AdvanceSpinner`, `StatusColumn:`, a `Frame`
  field or a glyph literal. Details in `docs/architecture/app-shell.md`.

Forbidden:
- ❌ A literal `Column{Indicator: …}` instead of `datatable.IndicatorColumn`
- ❌ A glyph literal (`"●"`, `"⊗"`) in a view: use `indicator.Glyph`
- ❌ A color chosen in the view for an activity state
- ❌ Green for a finished operation
- ❌ A color that depends on the type of operation

Forbidden:
- ❌ `.Align(lipgloss.Center)` on an icon column
- ❌ `.Align(lipgloss.Right)` on an icon column
- ❌ A title above a glyph column
- ❌ A local width (`colIconFixed`, `statusColumnWidth`, a literal `2`) instead of `datatable.IconColumnWidth`
- ❌ A glyph prefixed inside a text column's cell
- ❌ An icon color chosen in the view instead of a `theme.IconStyle` role
- ❌ A color table indexed by the glyph rather than by meaning
- ❌ An icon column with no `Style`, while the other three have one
- ❌ A role per file type where the row offers the same actions

### Rule 139 : A `datatable`'s body is never replaced — not by a spinner, not by a message

**A `datatable` stays a table, whatever it contains.** Whether it is
loading its data, empty because nothing has run yet, or empty because a
filter no longer matches anything, the rendered body is always
`m.table.View()` — header included, no rows. `datatable.View()` already
does this on its own: a zero-element table renders its header and fills
the rest with the background (`internal/ui/datatable/render.go`). Nothing
in a view therefore needs to detect this case.

What a body would have said instead — loading, the row count, a verdict —
is **the footer's and header's business**, never the body's:

- loading is a `components.Status{Text: "...", Spinner: true}` in the
  footer (Rule 128). That spinner is for the *table's data* loading; an
  operation on one row is the row's activity dot (Rule 125), never a spinner
  in the body;
- the row count, or whatever stands in for it (a verdict, a total), is a
  field of `GetHeaderInfo` (`shortcut.HeaderInfo{Key: "Images", Value: "0"}`) —
  it, not the body, answers "what am I looking at."

**Why.** A body that substitutes itself for the table — with a spinner or
with text — loses its header and its columns for as long as the condition
holds, then regains them: the layout jumps on every refresh, every
`ctrl+r`, every keystroke in the filter. The header and the footer, on the
other hand, have a fixed height (Rule 124): what they display changes
without ever moving the table.

```go
// ✅ CORRECT — the body is always the table; the footer and header speak
func (m Model) renderImagesView() string {
    return m.imageTable.View()
}

func (m Model) status() sharedcomponents.Status {
    if text, ok := m.loadingLabel(); ok {
        return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: text, Spinner: true}
    }
    return sharedcomponents.Status{Text: m.actionLine()}
}

func (m Model) GetHeaderInfo(_ string) []shortcut.HeaderInfo {
    return []shortcut.HeaderInfo{
        {Key: "Images", Value: fmt.Sprintf("%d", len(m.imageTable.Visible())), Style: theme.HeaderValueStyle},
    }
}

// ❌ WRONG — the body replaces itself with a spinner
if m.loading && len(m.images) == 0 {
    return theme.SpinnerMessage(m.spinner.View(), "Loading images...")
}

// ❌ WRONG — the body replaces itself with a message, empty or filtered
if len(m.imageTable.Visible()) == 0 {
    return theme.DimStyle.Render("No images found")
}
```

The spinner's frame is pushed from the `spinner.TickMsg` handler:
`m.footer.SetSpinnerFrame(m.spinner.View())`. Without this call the spinner
stays on frame zero, which reads as a hang.

`TestNoTableViewRendersALoadingBody` (`internal/ui/components`) rejects a
`theme.SpinnerMessage` in table views. An operation screen with no table
behind it (a `docker pull` in progress) is an exception **declared in the
test**.

**Declared exception: a welcome screen, not a status message.** The empty
`:sec` inventory (`internal/ui/security/inventory.go`, `renderEmptyInventory`)
replaces the body with a paragraph that explains *where scans come from* —
this is not "0 rows," it is first-use onboarding, with more content than a
header field can carry. The distinction: a message that fits in
`GetHeaderInfo` (a count, a status) goes there; text that explains an
entire application flow stays an explicit exception, like the one already
provided for loading.

### Rule 136 : Filter Bar for Tables

**Every table view must use `components.FilterBar` for search and toggle filters. No ad-hoc filter implementations.**

#### Behaviour

| State | Bar visible | Description |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| No filter | ❌ | Bar is completely hidden |
| Toggle filter active | ✅ | Bar shows dimmed placeholder + active token(s) |
| Search mode (after `/`) | ✅ | Bar shows focused text input + active token(s) |
| Search confirmed (query set) | ✅ | Bar shows dimmed placeholder + query token + toggle tokens |

#### Visual

The filter bar forms a **closed rectangle** that visually connects with the viewport's bottom border:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐   ← viewport top border
│  table rows...                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘   ← viewport bottom border (= rectangle top)
│  / cursor...         [tcp]  ·  [LISTEN] │   ← content line with │ sides
└─────────────────────────────────────────┘   ← rectangle bottom border
```

Both lines use `theme.ColorViewportBorder` for `│`, `└`, `┘`, `─` characters.

#### Placement — Footer, not viewport

The filter bar is rendered in `RenderFooter()`, **not** in the viewport content.

- `GetFooterHeight()` returns `baseFooterHeight + filterBar.ExtraHeight()`
- `RenderFooter()` prepends `filterBar.View()` when `filterBar.IsVisible()`
- Table height formula does **not** subtract `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` — the app router handles that via `GetFooterHeight()`

#### Integration Pattern

```go
// In Model struct
filterBar components.FilterBar  // or components.NewFilterBarWithTokens(tokens)

// In GetFooterHeight()
func (m Model) GetFooterHeight() int {
    return 2 + m.filterBar.ExtraHeight() // base (empty line + info) + filter bar
}

// In RenderFooter()
func (m Model) RenderFooter(width int) string {
    var parts []string
    if m.filterBar.IsVisible() {
        parts = append(parts, m.filterBar.View())
    }
    parts = append(parts, theme.EmptyLineBg(width), infoLine)
    return strings.Join(parts, "\n")
}

// In resize() / WindowSizeMsg handler — NO ExtraHeight subtraction
tableHeight := m.height - overhead  // overhead = header row only, NOT filterBar.ExtraHeight()
m.table.SetHeight(tableHeight)

// In Update() / key handler — forward keys when in search mode
if m.filterBar.InEditMode() {
    m.filterBar, cmd = m.filterBar.Update(msg)
    m.applyFilters()
    return m, cmd
}
// "/" key activates search
case "/":
    return m, m.filterBar.ActivateSearch()

// In InEditMode() — propagate to app router
func (m Model) InEditMode() bool {
    return m.filterBar.InEditMode() || /* other edit states */
}

// In View() / renderNormalView() — table only, NO filter bar here
func (m Model) renderNormalView() string {
    return m.table.View()
}

// In applyFilters() — use filterBar.SearchQuery() for text filtering
query := strings.ToLower(m.filterBar.SearchQuery())
```

#### Toggle filter tokens (views with dedicated filter keys)

Use `components.NewFilterBarWithTokens()` and update token active state when toggle keys are pressed:

```go
// Init
fb := components.NewFilterBarWithTokens([]components.FilterToken{
    {Label: "tcp"},
    {Label: "udp"},
})

// On key "t"
fb.SetTokenActive("tcp", !fb.IsTokenActive("tcp"))
```

#### Rules

- ✅ Use `components.FilterBar` — never re-implement the filter bar locally
- ✅ The frame itself is `components.BarFrame(width, inner)`: that is what
  `FilterBar.View()` calls, and the only path for whatever shares this slot
  without being a filter — the viewer's go-to-line prompt (§3.53). Two
  implementations of the rectangle would be free to diverge on where the
  corners sit.
- ✅ Only one occupant of the slot at a time, and the height does not depend
  on which one — otherwise the panel resizes under the reader whenever one
  opens on top of the other.
- ✅ `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` must be added to `GetFooterHeight()` return value
- ✅ `filterBar.View()` must be prepended in `RenderFooter()` when `filterBar.IsVisible()`
- ✅ `filterBar.InEditMode()` must propagate via the view's `InEditMode()` method
- ✅ `"/"` key must always call `filterBar.ActivateSearch()`
- ❌ Filter bar must NOT be rendered inside the viewport (`View()` / `renderNormalView()`)
- ❌ `filterBar.ExtraHeight()` must NOT be subtracted from table height (app router handles it)
- ❌ `filterInput textinput.Model` fields in view models (use FilterBar instead)

1127	### The broadcast, and the animation tick
1128	
1129	Views never hold a pointer to the registry. The router hands them a snapshot in
1130	`jobs.ChangedMsg`, so nothing is read from `View()` while something else writes
1131	it, and a view holding a snapshot cannot write back — every mutation goes
1132	through the one owner. `ChangedMsg.Failures` follows the same rule: a copy of
1133	the failure memory (above), never the registry's slice.
1134	
1135	**`ChangedMsg` is for changes of the registry, and carries no animation.**
1136	`broadcastJobs` updates **every held view**, on screen or not, so coming back to
1137	one shows what happened while it was away without it having to ask; the layout
1138	is re-measured once at the end, since only the view on screen can change the
1139	footer's height. A view built lazily on the way in was there for none of it, so
1140	every path that installs a view hands it the snapshot (`sendJobsTo`).
1141	
1142	**The animation travels in `jobs.FrameMsg`, to the view on screen only.** It
1143	carries `Frame` (bare, Rule 122: a table cell is measured before it is styled),
1144	`RenderedFrame` (styled, Rule 128: what a footer takes) and `Blink` (true is the
1145	"on" half). Only the router builds one (`frameMsg`, in `internal/app/animation.go`).
1146	Before DEVDESK-139 the frame rode in `ChangedMsg` and every tick made every held
1147	view rebuild its rows; now a tick touches one view. `enterView` (snapshot plus
1148	current frame) is called wherever a view takes the screen: `switchView`,
1149	`openBrowser`, the path picker, `openSecurityView`, `rescanInOrigin` and
1150	`returnToOrigin`. Without it a view would show the previous frame, or an "off"
1151	phase, until the next tick.
1152	
1153	#### One tick, one chain
1154	
1155	There is **one** animation chain for the whole application (D5, renamed
1156	"animation" by D2; it used to be the spinner chain): `animationTickMsg{seq, at}`,
1157	started only by `ensureTick`, renewed only by `handleAnimationTick`
1158	(`TestTheRouterHasOneAnimationChain` enforces both). It is built on `tea.Every`,
1159	so ticks land on the clock's boundaries and the blink alternates strictly.
1160	
1161	`App.Update` is a thin wrapper: it runs `update` (the dispatch), then
1162	`ensureTick`. The check is a **level**, not an edge — it runs after every
1163	message, so no handler has to remember to start a chain, and it is idempotent
1164	within one `Update`.
1165	
1166	| Need | Cadence |
1167	|---|---|
1168	| `jobs.Running() > 0` (footer spinners depend on the frame) | 100 ms (`spinner.Dot.FPS`) |
1169	| the view on screen has nothing running but `WantsBlink()` (`BlinkingView`) | 500 ms |
1170	| the terminal is blurred (`terminalBlurred`), whatever the two above say | no chain |
1171	| neither, or `motionStatic` with no running work | no chain |
1172	
1173	`BlinkingView` sits beside `FormView` and `LeavingView`: an optional interface for
1174	a row that blinks for a reason the registry does not know (an instant action, an
1175	agent running, children loading). The router asks the view on screen after every
1176	`Update`.
1177	
1178	- **Seq.** A tick of a chain that was replaced is dropped without a Cmd, so a
1179	  second chain is impossible rather than merely unlikely.
1180	- **Faster need.** `ensureTick` replaces a slower live chain (`seq++`), never
1181	  adds a second.
1182	- **Slower need.** The live chain downgrades at its next renewal, without a new
1183	  seq. When no cadence is wanted it is not renewed and dies.
1184	- **Phase.** Read off the tick's own time, not a counter:
1185	  `(t.UnixMilli()/500)%2 == 0` is on. Every view blinks in step whatever the
1186	  interval the chain runs at (1 Hz).
1187	- **Frame.** Advances only while `Running() > 0`.
1188	- **At rest the phase is forced "on".** When the chain stops on an "off" phase,
1189	  the router pins it on and sends one last `FrameMsg` to the view on screen: a
1190	  settled row is left on a steady glyph, never a half-blinked one.
1191	- **`motionStatic`.** Pins the phase on and keeps blink-only chains from
1192	  starting (`setMotionStatic` hands the pinned frame to the view on screen at
1193	  once). `app.motion` feeds `App.motionStatic` through `applyMotion`: at
1194	  startup (`newWithSize`), after a context switch (`handleContextSwitchComplete`,
1195	  once the views are rebuilt) and on `ConfigSavedMsg` (`handleConfigSaved`).
1196	
1197	`jobsChanged` is what a launch site or a transition calls after writing to the
1198	registry: `ChangedMsg` to every held view, `FrameMsg` to the view on screen. The
1199	`Update` wrapper then makes sure a chain is alive; the three are separate, and
1200	none implies another.
1201	
1202	This is what removes the four hand-stamped frames, and with them the failure
1203	each of them could produce: a chain that died on the first idle tick with
1204	nothing able to restart it, leaving the spinner frozen on the frame it died at.
1205	
1206	#### Terminal focus (DEVDESK-210)
1207	
1208	Bubble Tea v2 reports whether the terminal has the focus (xterm mode 1004) when
1209	the view asks for it. The router uses it to stop the animation chain while the
1210	terminal is blurred, and to tell the view on screen so it can skip its periodic
1211	reads (see "Routing the level to a view").
1212	
1213	- **Asking.** `App.View` is the only place that sets `ReportFocus`. A view's
1214	  `View()` never does, like `AltScreen` and `BackgroundColor`.
1215	- **The level.** `App.terminalBlurred` is a bool whose zero value means
1216	  focused. `tea.BlurMsg` sets it (`handleTerminalBlur`), `tea.FocusMsg` clears
1217	  it (`handleTerminalFocus`). Neither returns a Cmd.
1218	- **The cadence.** `ensureTick` and `handleAnimationTick` read `wantedCadence`,
1219	  not `cadence` directly. While blurred it answers "no chain", whatever the
1220	  registry or the view on screen asks for; otherwise it is `cadence(...)`.
1221	  `cadence()` itself is unchanged.
1222	- **No seq bump on blur.** The in-flight tick still arrives, finds that no
1223	  cadence is wanted and does not renew the chain, so the chain dies by itself.
1224	  A blur always hands the view one last `FrameMsg` with the phase pinned on,
1225	  so a row is never left on a half-blinked glyph. After a focus, the `Update`
1226	  wrapper's `ensureTick` starts one chain. If the focus comes before the
1227	  in-flight tick lands, that tick renews the chain: still one chain.
1228	- **Not relayed.** `BlurMsg` and `FocusMsg` are not forwarded to any view.
1229	  Forwarding a raw focus would make `bubbles/cursor` restart its blink on
1230	  cursors the view never meant to show.
1231	- **Jobs are untouched.** A blur never cancels, pauses or delays a job:
1232	  `jobs.Running()`, the registry and its broadcasts (`ChangedMsg`, failures
1233	  included) work as usual. Only the animation stops.
1234	
1235	**Routing the level to a view (step 2).** The router does not relay the raw
1236	events (see "Not relayed"). It sends the view its own message,
1237	`shared.TerminalFocusMsg{Focused, Resume}` (`internal/shared/focus.go`), built
1238	by `App.sendFocusTo` (`internal/app/focus.go`). Five views consume it:
1239	`:agent-usage`, `:containers`, `:net` (Ports poll), the dashboard and `:oci`;
1240	their behaviour is in `agent-usage.md`, `network.md` and `ui-components.md`.
1241	
1242	- **Who receives it.** Only the view on screen (`a.currentView`). A view the
1243	  router keeps but does not show gets nothing, so a retained view never learns
1244	  of a blur while it is hidden.
1245	- **`Focused`** is `!suspended()` at the time of sending (see "The
1246	  `when_unfocused` policy" below): true whenever the terminal has the focus, and
1247	  also while it is blurred under `run`.
1248	- **`Resume`** is true only on the focus edge that follows a blur. It tells
1249	  the view it may catch up on what it paused (a refresh tick, for example). It
1250	  is never true while blurred.
1251	- **When it is sent.**
1252	  - On the blur edge: `Focused:false, Resume:false` (`handleTerminalBlur`).
1253	  - On the focus edge after a blur: `Focused:true, Resume:true`
1254	    (`handleTerminalFocus`).
1255	  - When a view enters the screen: `enterView` sends the current level with
1256	    `Resume:false`, next to the jobs snapshot and the frame.
1257	  - After `reinitializeViews` rebuilds the views, with the current level and
1258	    `Resume:false`, so a rebuilt view does not start unaware of a blur still
1259	    in effect.
1260	- **A key or a paste while blurred** counts as the focus coming back (see
1261	  below). `update` keeps the Cmd of that `Resume:true` message and batches it
1262	  with the Cmd of the key or paste handler (`tea.Batch`), so neither is lost.
1263	- **What it never does.** It calls no `Init`, starts no scan and sets no
1264	  footer message. What a view does with it is the view's choice.
1265	
1266	*Known limit.* Only the paths that go through `enterView` hand the level to
1267	the incoming view. These paths change `a.currentView` without it, so the view
1268	they show is not told the level: the viewer (`viewer.go`), netdiag
1269	(`netdiag.go`), the context switch (`context.go`) and the returns from the
1270	file picker and from selection mode (`picker.go`, `selection.go`). If the
1271	terminal is blurred when one of them runs, that view assumes it is focused
1272	until the next edge. Closing this gap is not part of step 2.
1273	
1274	Two hypotheses keep a lost or missing event from leaving the router wrong:
1275	
1276	- **A `FocusMsg` with no prior blur does nothing.** `Update` returns at once,
1277	  with no Cmd: an unknown focus means focused.
1278	- **A key press or a paste while blurred counts as the focus coming back.**
1279	  `update` runs `handleTerminalFocus` before dispatching it. This heals a lost
1280	  focus-in (a tmux pane switch, or a hand-off to a child process, see
1281	  [Handing the terminal to a child](#handing-the-terminal-to-a-child--internaluiteaexec)).
1282	
1283	**The `when_unfocused` policy.** `app.when_unfocused` (`pause`, the default, or
1284	`run`; see `configuration.md`) decides whether a blur suspends anything.
1285	`App.runWhenUnfocused` holds it, read from the config by `RunsWhenUnfocused()`.
1286	`App.suspended()` is `terminalBlurred && !runWhenUnfocused`. Everything above
1287	that stops on a blur reads `suspended()`, not `terminalBlurred`: `wantedCadence`,
1288	the pinned last frame, and the `Focused` and `Resume` fields of
1289	`TerminalFocusMsg` (`Resume` is `resume && !suspended()`). With `run`, nothing is
1290	suspended: the animation chain keeps going and every view gets `Focused:true`.
1291	`terminalBlurred` itself still tracks the real focus.
1292	
1293	The setting applies without a restart. `applyWhenUnfocused` runs on
1294	`ConfigSavedMsg` and on a context switch. If the policy changes while the
1295	terminal is blurred, the view on screen is told at once (`pause` to `run`:
1296	resumed; `run` to `pause`: suspended).
1297	
1298	**Degradation.** A terminal without mode 1004 never sends `BlurMsg`, so
1299	`terminalBlurred` stays false and the application behaves as before. Under tmux
1300	the host needs `set -g focus-events on`; without it tmux swallows the events and
1301	DevDesk never sees a blur. A terminal that is visible but not focused (a side
1302	pane) is treated as blurred: its animation and periodic reads stop, unless
1303	`app.when_unfocused` is `run`.
1304	
1305	#### A row dot or a loading spinner
1306	
1307	Two things move on screen, and they answer different questions:
1308	
1309	| | Says | Where | Driven by |
1310	|---|---|---|---|
1311	| activity dot (`●`/`○`) | an operation is running **on this row's target** | column 0 of a table (Rule 125) | the registry (`jobs`), or a `MarkBusy` key, read at render; blink phase from the shared tick |
1312	| loading spinner | **the view is fetching its data** (a list, a tab, a refresh) | the footer, `components.Status{Spinner: true}` (Rules 128, 139) | the view's own `spinner.Model`, which turns only while it loads |
1313	
1314	A view never draws a spinner in a row: the per-row spinner chains
1315	(`AdvanceSpinner`, `busyTick`, a node spinner) were deleted by the migrations
1316	(DEVDESK-139 to 153) and `StatusColumn` with them (DEVDESK-143). The loading
1317	spinner is the only animation left that a view owns; it stops on `!loading` and
1318	is not the router's chain. When the selected row has a footer detail with a
1319	glyph, the footer spinner is not shown: the row's dot already moves.
1320	
1321	#### Row chains outside the router
1322	
1323	No row-animation chain lives in a view: `TestNoRowAnimationChainOutsideTheRouter`
1324	scans every source file outside `ui/datatable/` and fails on a row chain
1325	(`AdvanceSpinner`, `portsSpinnerCmd`, a `tagScanSpinnerIdx` step), with no list
1326	of declared chains to extend. `TestOnlyTheRouterBuildsAFrameMsg` and
1327	`TestTheAnimationChainUnderARealProgram` (a real `tea.Program`, meant for
1328	`-race`) complete the guard rails.
1329	
1330	#### What the redraw costs
1331	
1332	`DEVDESK_MEASURE_REDRAW=1 go test ./internal/app -run TestMeasureRedrawCost -v`
1333	counts the bytes Bubble Tea's renderer writes to an `io.Writer` on a simulated
1334	120x40 terminal — not a real terminal. Opt-in; the test is skipped otherwise.
1335	
1336	| Animation | Bytes emitted |
1337	|---|---|
1338	| no animated row | 0 B/s |
1339	| 1 row blinking at 1 Hz | 376 B/s |
1340	| 20 rows blinking at 1 Hz | 5 809 B/s |
1341	| reference: spinner at 10 Hz, 1 row | 1 880 B/s |
1342	| reference: spinner at 10 Hz, 20 rows | 29 049 B/s |
1343	
1344	Nothing animated costs nothing, and a 1 Hz blink costs about a fifth of the
1345	10 Hz spinner it sits beside.
1346	
1347	
1348	### The `:jobs` view — `internal/ui/jobsview`
1349	
1350	The reader's side of the registry, and it owns nothing: it starts no work, holds
1351	no timer and fetches nothing. Its rows are the snapshot, so there is nothing to
1352	refresh — `ctrl+r` is absent rather than greyed, because there is no operation
1353	behind it to be unavailable.
1354	
1355	Two levels (D2): the runs, and `→` on one of them for its targets. A level
1356	rather than a pair of tabs — the second table is *about* a row of the first, so
1357	it is reached the way every drill-down in the application is (Rule 111), and the
1358	trail is a breadcrumb below the table (Rule 123).
1359	
1360	| | Columns |
1361	|---|---|
1362	| runs | activity indicator (untitled, `IconColumnWidth`), Kind, Label, Progress, State, Started |
1363	| targets | activity indicator, Target, State, Detail |
1364	
1365	**Column 0 is the activity indicator** (DEVDESK-142, Rule 125), built by
1366	`datatable.IndicatorColumn` over `components.RunIndicator` / `ItemIndicator`
1367	(`job_activity.go`): queued `◴`, running `●`/`○`, done `◉`, failed `⊗`,
1368	cancelled `⊘`, skipped `⊖`. It is the state, not the kind: a jobs list is
1369	scanned for the run that failed and the one still going. The Kind column
1370	carries the state in its `Search` so `/failed` and `/scan` both work while the
1371	glyph column stays out of the filter. The State word takes the dot's colour
1372	(`indicator.Style`), so the row has one colour source; `done` is neutral, not
1373	green, and queued, cancelled and skipped now share that neutral colour.
1374	
1375	**The blink phase is read at render.** The rows carry nothing animated:
1376	`runRow`/`itemRow` wrap the record only. `jobs.FrameMsg` calls
1377	`SetBlinkPhase(msg.Blink)` on both tables and pushes the footer spinner frame;
1378	no row is rebuilt (`SetItems` stays the only way rows are rebuilt, from
1379	`ChangedMsg`). A queued run no longer spins: it shows a fixed `◴`.
1380	
1381	**The footer says the selected row.** `status()` fills `Status.Detail` with
1382	`components.DescribeRun` (or `DescribeItem` at the target level) of the row
1383	under the cursor, and keeps `N jobs running` as the text. The footer spinner is
1384	shown only when no detail is, since the row's own dot moves. A `Warn` (a refused
1385	`K` or `.`) keeps priority over the detail and the detail returns when it
1386	expires. The help ends with `indicator.Legend(indicator.JobsLegend...)`.
1387	
1388	**The context is passed, not read.** `jobsview.New(cfg, contextName)` takes the
1389	name from the router, for D68's reason one screen over: the router is what knows
1390	which context is current. The view filters the snapshot on it (`FilterContext`),
1391	so a switch hides runs rather than dropping them — and the router rebuilds every
1392	view on a switch anyway, so the cached name cannot go stale.
1393	
1394	`K` is state-aware at both levels (Rule 130) and greyed with a **named** reason:
1395	"This run has already finished", "A delete cannot be stopped once it has
1396	started". The refusal is never silent — pressing a greyed key says why in the
1397	footer.
1398	
1399	**The dashboard gained the counter** the same way, and it is the one screen that
1400	always gets D9's degraded form: it launches nothing, so it passes no origin, and
1401	`2 jobs running — :jobs for details` is the whole of what it can honestly say.
1402	The sentence itself is `components.JobsStatusLine`, shared with the workspaces
1403	footer — two copies of a deliberate surrender would each have been free to
1404	surrender differently.
1405	
1406	### Handing the terminal to a child — `internal/ui/teaexec`
1407	
1408	**The race (Bubble Tea v2.1.1, DEVDESK-290).** Bubble Tea's exec path is
1409	`stopRenderer`, `ExecCommand.Run`, `startRenderer`. `stopRenderer` sends on an
1410	unbuffered channel: it returns when the render goroutine has received the signal,
1411	not when it has finished, and that goroutine then runs `ticker.Stop()` on its
1412	own. `startRenderer` reuses the same ticker (`Reset`). When the child returns at
1413	once (failed start, missing binary), `Reset` can run before the late `Stop()`:
1414	the ticker stays stopped and the screen never repaints while the program keeps
1415	handling input. Nothing in the `ExecCallback` can fix it, because the callback
1416	runs after the race is decided.
1417	
1418	**The workaround.** `settled.Run` runs the child, then sleeps for whatever remains
1419	of `settleDelay` (50 ms since `Run` started), also when the child failed, and
1420	returns the child's error unchanged. The old render goroutine has time to stop
1421	the ticker before `startRenderer` resets it. The delay is in `Run`, not in the
1422	callback, for the reason above. A child that lasts 50 ms or more pays nothing;
1423	the worst cost is 50 ms. The delay is probabilistic, but the tests below check
1424	it.
1425	
1426	**The API.** `teaexec.Process(*exec.Cmd, tea.ExecCallback)` replaces
1427	`tea.ExecProcess`; `teaexec.Command(tea.ExecCommand, tea.ExecCallback)` replaces
1428	`tea.Exec`. Both return a `tea.Cmd`. `Process` sets a stream only when it is
1429	nil, like Bubble Tea's own `osExecCommand`.
1430	
1431	**The rule.** No code outside the package calls `tea.ExecProcess`, `tea.Exec` or
1432	`tea.Suspend`. `source_guard_test.go` (`TestNoDirectTeaExecOutsideTeaexec`) scans
1433	the repository's Go files and fails on a direct call, by file and line; its
1434	helper is unit-tested on positive and negative cases. A comment or an unrelated
1435	`Exec` method does not trip it.
1436	
1437	**The tests.** `program_test.go` runs a real `tea.Program` at `GOMAXPROCS(1)`,
1438	where the loss is deterministic. `TestARedrawFollowsAnInstantChild` (20 runs) and
1439	`TestARedrawFollowsAChildThatFailsAtOnce` check that the view is drawn again
1440	after the child. Trap: `tea.WithInput(nil)` makes every exec wait 500 ms before
1441	the child starts, so the waits in those tests are generous.
1442	
1443	**The sentinel.** `TestUpstreamTickerRaceStillExists` runs a bare `tea.Exec` and
1444	expects the redraw to be lost. When it fails ("Bubble Tea no longer loses the
1445	renderer ticker"), upstream fixed the race: the wrapper can be removed.
1446	Replace `teaexec.Process` and `teaexec.Command` with the Bubble Tea calls, delete
1447	the package and the source guard, and update this section.
1448	
1449	### The activity-column guard (DEVDESK-142, A-16 skeleton)
1450	
1451	`internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` keeps every view on the activity column
1452	(Rule 125) and keeps it there. It classifies every `command.ViewType` into one of
1453	two lists, **per table**: a view is migrated or exempt, never both and never
1454	neither. There is no list of tables waiting for their story any more (DEVDESK-143
1455	closed it) and no exception to shrink:
1456	
1457	| List | Meaning |
1458	|---|---|
1459	| `migratedTables` | the view's tables are on the activity column (`:jobs`: `jobs/runs`, `jobs/targets`; ws: `ws`; `:sec`: `sec/inventory`; OCI: `oci/images`, `oci/networks`, `oci/volumes`, `oci/registries`, `oci/registry-browser`; explorer: `explorer/tree`, `explorer/clone-list`; templates: `templates`; netdiag: `netdiag/ports`; `:agent-usage`: `agent-usage/agents`; containers: `containers`) |
1460	| `exemptViews` | views with no activity to show (dashboard, status, git-auth, configuration, about, files, viewer), each with its reason |
1461	
1462	A view in neither list, or an exempt view that is also migrated, fails by name (`classificationProblems`, unit-tested on fictitious classifications). A migrated view
1463	exposes `ActivityTables() map[string]datatable.ActivityTable` (a read-only face:
1464	`Shapes()` and `RenderedWidth()`, see `ui-components.md`); an exempt view that reports any table fails with "remove the exception".
1465	
1466	The netdiag view's `migratedSources` are two files only, `ports_model.go` and `ports_activity.go` (DEVDESK-150): netdiag migrates its Ports tab alone, and the guard scans the files that belong to it. `ports_commands.go` is left out: its `portsTickCmd` is the data refresh tick, not a row animation (same reasoning as OCI's `commands.go`). 1467	
1468	The `:agent-usage` view's `migratedSources` is the whole `ui/agentusageview/` package (no `tea.Tick` in it: `pollTickCmd` sleeps inside a `Cmd`), it reports `agent-usage/agents` from `ActivityTables()` and implements `WantsBlink()`; its footer seed (`seedAgentUsageFooter`) puts a transcript with a fresh line on disk and expects `indicator.Running`, without running the 2 s poll `Cmd`.

1470	The templates view's `migratedSources` is the whole `ui/templates/` package; it reports `templates` from `ActivityTables()` and has a footer seed (a sync running on the selected row).
1471	
1472	The explorer's `migratedSources` is the whole `explorer` package (no frame or `jobFrame` left in it). The registry side adds `jobs.SafeCause` (credentials removed from a cause) and `jobs.CancelledDetail`.
1473	
1474	**Checked at run time**, on each view built by the router: column 0 of every
1475	migrated table is the indicator (untitled, fixed, `IconColumnWidth`, no `Less`,
1476	no `Search`); `RenderedWidth()` equals `width-2` after a 60-column resize
1477	(Rule 116); the help holds the `indicator.Legend` section.
1478	
1479	**Checked by source analysis**, on migrated packages only (`ui/jobsview/`, `ui/workspaces/`, `ui/security/`): no
1480	`AdvanceSpinner` call, no `StatusColumn:` key, no `Frame`/`frame`/`SpinnerFrame`

### The broadcast, and the animation tick

Views never hold a pointer to the registry. The router hands them a snapshot in
`jobs.ChangedMsg`, so nothing is read from `View()` while something else writes
it, and a view holding a snapshot cannot write back — every mutation goes
through the one owner. `ChangedMsg.Failures` follows the same rule: a copy of
the failure memory (above), never the registry's slice.

**`ChangedMsg` is for changes of the registry, and carries no animation.**
`broadcastJobs` updates **every held view**, on screen or not, so coming back to
one shows what happened while it was away without it having to ask; the layout
is re-measured once at the end, since only the view on screen can change the
footer's height. A view built lazily on the way in was there for none of it, so
every path that installs a view hands it the snapshot (`sendJobsTo`).

**The animation travels in `jobs.FrameMsg`, to the view on screen only.** It
carries `Frame` (bare, Rule 122: a table cell is measured before it is styled),
`RenderedFrame` (styled, Rule 128: what a footer takes) and `Blink` (true is the
"on" half). Only the router builds one (`frameMsg`, in `internal/app/animation.go`).
Before DEVDESK-139 the frame rode in `ChangedMsg` and every tick made every held
view rebuild its rows; now a tick touches one view. `enterView` (snapshot plus
current frame) is called wherever a view takes the screen: `switchView`,
`openBrowser`, the path picker, `openSecurityView`, `rescanInOrigin` and
`returnToOrigin`. Without it a view would show the previous frame, or an "off"
phase, until the next tick.

#### One tick, one chain

There is **one** animation chain for the whole application (D5, renamed
"animation" by D2; it used to be the spinner chain): `animationTickMsg{seq, at}`,
started only by `ensureTick`, renewed only by `handleAnimationTick`
(`TestTheRouterHasOneAnimationChain` enforces both). It is built on `tea.Every`,
so ticks land on the clock's boundaries and the blink alternates strictly.

`App.Update` is a thin wrapper: it runs `update` (the dispatch), then
`ensureTick`. The check is a **level**, not an edge — it runs after every
message, so no handler has to remember to start a chain, and it is idempotent
within one `Update`.

| Need | Cadence |
|---|---|
| `jobs.Running() > 0` (footer spinners depend on the frame) | 100 ms (`spinner.Dot.FPS`) |
| the view on screen has nothing running but `WantsBlink()` (`BlinkingView`) | 500 ms |
| the terminal is blurred (`terminalBlurred`), whatever the two above say | no chain |
| neither, or `motionStatic` with no running work | no chain |

`BlinkingView` sits beside `FormView` and `LeavingView`: an optional interface for
a row that blinks for a reason the registry does not know (an instant action, an
agent running, children loading). The router asks the view on screen after every
`Update`.

- **Seq.** A tick of a chain that was replaced is dropped without a Cmd, so a
  second chain is impossible rather than merely unlikely.
- **Faster need.** `ensureTick` replaces a slower live chain (`seq++`), never
  adds a second.
- **Slower need.** The live chain downgrades at its next renewal, without a new
  seq. When no cadence is wanted it is not renewed and dies.
- **Phase.** Read off the tick's own time, not a counter:
  `(t.UnixMilli()/500)%2 == 0` is on. Every view blinks in step whatever the
  interval the chain runs at (1 Hz).
- **Frame.** Advances only while `Running() > 0`.
- **At rest the phase is forced "on".** When the chain stops on an "off" phase,
  the router pins it on and sends one last `FrameMsg` to the view on screen: a
  settled row is left on a steady glyph, never a half-blinked one.
- **`motionStatic`.** Pins the phase on and keeps blink-only chains from
  starting (`setMotionStatic` hands the pinned frame to the view on screen at
  once). `app.motion` feeds `App.motionStatic` through `applyMotion`: at
  startup (`newWithSize`), after a context switch (`handleContextSwitchComplete`,
  once the views are rebuilt) and on `ConfigSavedMsg` (`handleConfigSaved`).

`jobsChanged` is what a launch site or a transition calls after writing to the
registry: `ChangedMsg` to every held view, `FrameMsg` to the view on screen. The
`Update` wrapper then makes sure a chain is alive; the three are separate, and
none implies another.

This is what removes the four hand-stamped frames, and with them the failure
each of them could produce: a chain that died on the first idle tick with
nothing able to restart it, leaving the spinner frozen on the frame it died at.

#### Terminal focus (DEVDESK-210)

Bubble Tea v2 reports whether the terminal has the focus (xterm mode 1004) when
the view asks for it. The router uses it to stop the animation chain while the
terminal is blurred, and to tell the view on screen so it can skip its periodic
reads (see "Routing the level to a view").

- **Asking.** `App.View` is the only place that sets `ReportFocus`. A view's
  `View()` never does, like `AltScreen` and `BackgroundColor`.
- **The level.** `App.terminalBlurred` is a bool whose zero value means
  focused. `tea.BlurMsg` sets it (`handleTerminalBlur`), `tea.FocusMsg` clears
  it (`handleTerminalFocus`). Neither returns a Cmd.
- **The cadence.** `ensureTick` and `handleAnimationTick` read `wantedCadence`,
  not `cadence` directly. While blurred it answers "no chain", whatever the
  registry or the view on screen asks for; otherwise it is `cadence(...)`.
  `cadence()` itself is unchanged.
- **No seq bump on blur.** The in-flight tick still arrives, finds that no
  cadence is wanted and does not renew the chain, so the chain dies by itself.
  A blur always hands the view one last `FrameMsg` with the phase pinned on,
  so a row is never left on a half-blinked glyph. After a focus, the `Update`
  wrapper's `ensureTick` starts one chain. If the focus comes before the
  in-flight tick lands, that tick renews the chain: still one chain.
- **Not relayed.** `BlurMsg` and `FocusMsg` are not forwarded to any view.
  Forwarding a raw focus would make `bubbles/cursor` restart its blink on
  cursors the view never meant to show.
- **Jobs are untouched.** A blur never cancels, pauses or delays a job:
  `jobs.Running()`, the registry and its broadcasts (`ChangedMsg`, failures
  included) work as usual. Only the animation stops.

**Routing the level to a view (step 2).** The router does not relay the raw
events (see "Not relayed"). It sends the view its own message,
`shared.TerminalFocusMsg{Focused, Resume}` (`internal/shared/focus.go`), built
by `App.sendFocusTo` (`internal/app/focus.go`). Five views consume it:
`:agent-usage`, `:containers`, `:net` (Ports poll), the dashboard and `:oci`;
their behaviour is in `agent-usage.md`, `network.md` and `ui-components.md`.

- **Who receives it.** Only the view on screen (`a.currentView`). A view the
  router keeps but does not show gets nothing, so a retained view never learns
  of a blur while it is hidden.
- **`Focused`** is `!suspended()` at the time of sending (see "The
  `when_unfocused` policy" below): true whenever the terminal has the focus, and
  also while it is blurred under `run`.
- **`Resume`** is true only on the focus edge that follows a blur. It tells
  the view it may catch up on what it paused (a refresh tick, for example). It
  is never true while blurred.
- **When it is sent.**
  - On the blur edge: `Focused:false, Resume:false` (`handleTerminalBlur`).
  - On the focus edge after a blur: `Focused:true, Resume:true`
    (`handleTerminalFocus`).
  - When a view enters the screen: `enterView` sends the current level with
    `Resume:false`, next to the jobs snapshot and the frame.
  - After `reinitializeViews` rebuilds the views, with the current level and
    `Resume:false`, so a rebuilt view does not start unaware of a blur still
    in effect.
- **A key or a paste while blurred** counts as the focus coming back (see
  below). `update` keeps the Cmd of that `Resume:true` message and batches it
  with the Cmd of the key or paste handler (`tea.Batch`), so neither is lost.
- **What it never does.** It calls no `Init`, starts no scan and sets no
  footer message. What a view does with it is the view's choice.

*Known limit.* Only the paths that go through `enterView` hand the level to
the incoming view. These paths change `a.currentView` without it, so the view
they show is not told the level: the viewer (`viewer.go`), netdiag
(`netdiag.go`), the context switch (`context.go`) and the returns from the
file picker and from selection mode (`picker.go`, `selection.go`). If the
terminal is blurred when one of them runs, that view assumes it is focused
until the next edge. Closing this gap is not part of step 2.

Two hypotheses keep a lost or missing event from leaving the router wrong:

- **A `FocusMsg` with no prior blur does nothing.** `Update` returns at once,
  with no Cmd: an unknown focus means focused.
- **A key press or a paste while blurred counts as the focus coming back.**
  `update` runs `handleTerminalFocus` before dispatching it. This heals a lost
  focus-in (a tmux pane switch, or a hand-off to a child process, see
  [Handing the terminal to a child](#handing-the-terminal-to-a-child--internaluiteaexec)).

**The `when_unfocused` policy.** `app.when_unfocused` (`pause`, the default, or
`run`; see `configuration.md`) decides whether a blur suspends anything.
`App.runWhenUnfocused` holds it, read from the config by `RunsWhenUnfocused()`.
`App.suspended()` is `terminalBlurred && !runWhenUnfocused`. Everything above
that stops on a blur reads `suspended()`, not `terminalBlurred`: `wantedCadence`,
the pinned last frame, and the `Focused` and `Resume` fields of
`TerminalFocusMsg` (`Resume` is `resume && !suspended()`). With `run`, nothing is
suspended: the animation chain keeps going and every view gets `Focused:true`.
`terminalBlurred` itself still tracks the real focus.

The setting applies without a restart. `applyWhenUnfocused` runs on
`ConfigSavedMsg` and on a context switch. If the policy changes while the
terminal is blurred, the view on screen is told at once (`pause` to `run`:
resumed; `run` to `pause`: suspended).

**Degradation.** A terminal without mode 1004 never sends `BlurMsg`, so
`terminalBlurred` stays false and the application behaves as before. Under tmux
the host needs `set -g focus-events on`; without it tmux swallows the events and
DevDesk never sees a blur. A terminal that is visible but not focused (a side
pane) is treated as blurred: its animation and periodic reads stop, unless
`app.when_unfocused` is `run`.

#### A row dot or a loading spinner

Two things move on screen, and they answer different questions:

| | Says | Where | Driven by |
|---|---|---|---|
| activity dot (`●`/`○`) | an operation is running **on this row's target** | column 0 of a table (Rule 125) | the registry (`jobs`), or a `MarkBusy` key, read at render; blink phase from the shared tick |
| loading spinner | **the view is fetching its data** (a list, a tab, a refresh) | the footer, `components.Status{Spinner: true}` (Rules 128, 139) | the view's own `spinner.Model`, which turns only while it loads |

A view never draws a spinner in a row: the per-row spinner chains
(`AdvanceSpinner`, `busyTick`, a node spinner) were deleted by the migrations
(DEVDESK-139 to 153) and `StatusColumn` with them (DEVDESK-143). The loading
spinner is the only animation left that a view owns; it stops on `!loading` and
is not the router's chain. When the selected row has a footer detail with a
glyph, the footer spinner is not shown: the row's dot already moves.

#### Row chains outside the router

No row-animation chain lives in a view: `TestNoRowAnimationChainOutsideTheRouter`
scans every source file outside `ui/datatable/` and fails on a row chain
(`AdvanceSpinner`, `portsSpinnerCmd`, a `tagScanSpinnerIdx` step), with no list
of declared chains to extend. `TestOnlyTheRouterBuildsAFrameMsg` and
`TestTheAnimationChainUnderARealProgram` (a real `tea.Program`, meant for
`-race`) complete the guard rails.

#### What the redraw costs

`DEVDESK_MEASURE_REDRAW=1 go test ./internal/app -run TestMeasureRedrawCost -v`
counts the bytes Bubble Tea's renderer writes to an `io.Writer` on a simulated
120x40 terminal — not a real terminal. Opt-in; the test is skipped otherwise.

| Animation | Bytes emitted |
|---|---|
| no animated row | 0 B/s |
| 1 row blinking at 1 Hz | 376 B/s |
| 20 rows blinking at 1 Hz | 5 809 B/s |
| reference: spinner at 10 Hz, 1 row | 1 880 B/s |
| reference: spinner at 10 Hz, 20 rows | 29 049 B/s |

Nothing animated costs nothing, and a 1 Hz blink costs about a fifth of the
10 Hz spinner it sits beside.


### The `:jobs` view — `internal/ui/jobsview`

The reader's side of the registry, and it owns nothing: it starts no work, holds
no timer and fetches nothing. Its rows are the snapshot, so there is nothing to
refresh — `ctrl+r` is absent rather than greyed, because there is no operation
behind it to be unavailable.

Two levels (D2): the runs, and `→` on one of them for its targets. A level
rather than a pair of tabs — the second table is *about* a row of the first, so
it is reached the way every drill-down in the application is (Rule 111), and the
trail is a breadcrumb below the table (Rule 123).

| | Columns |
|---|---|
| runs | activity indicator (untitled, `IconColumnWidth`), Kind, Label, Progress, State, Started |
| targets | activity indicator, Target, State, Detail |

**Column 0 is the activity indicator** (DEVDESK-142, Rule 125), built by
`datatable.IndicatorColumn` over `components.RunIndicator` / `ItemIndicator`
(`job_activity.go`): queued `◴`, running `●`/`○`, done `◉`, failed `⊗`,
cancelled `⊘`, skipped `⊖`. It is the state, not the kind: a jobs list is
scanned for the run that failed and the one still going. The Kind column
carries the state in its `Search` so `/failed` and `/scan` both work while the
glyph column stays out of the filter. The State word takes the dot's colour
(`indicator.Style`), so the row has one colour source; `done` is neutral, not
green, and queued, cancelled and skipped now share that neutral colour.

**The blink phase is read at render.** The rows carry nothing animated:
`runRow`/`itemRow` wrap the record only. `jobs.FrameMsg` calls
`SetBlinkPhase(msg.Blink)` on both tables and pushes the footer spinner frame;
no row is rebuilt (`SetItems` stays the only way rows are rebuilt, from
`ChangedMsg`). A queued run no longer spins: it shows a fixed `◴`.

**The footer says the selected row.** `status()` fills `Status.Detail` with
`components.DescribeRun` (or `DescribeItem` at the target level) of the row
under the cursor, and keeps `N jobs running` as the text. The footer spinner is
shown only when no detail is, since the row's own dot moves. A `Warn` (a refused
`K` or `.`) keeps priority over the detail and the detail returns when it
expires. The help ends with `indicator.Legend(indicator.JobsLegend...)`.

**The context is passed, not read.** `jobsview.New(cfg, contextName)` takes the
name from the router, for D68's reason one screen over: the router is what knows
which context is current. The view filters the snapshot on it (`FilterContext`),
so a switch hides runs rather than dropping them — and the router rebuilds every
view on a switch anyway, so the cached name cannot go stale.

`K` is state-aware at both levels (Rule 130) and greyed with a **named** reason:
"This run has already finished", "A delete cannot be stopped once it has
started". The refusal is never silent — pressing a greyed key says why in the
footer.

**The dashboard gained the counter** the same way, and it is the one screen that
always gets D9's degraded form: it launches nothing, so it passes no origin, and
`2 jobs running — :jobs for details` is the whole of what it can honestly say.
The sentence itself is `components.JobsStatusLine`, shared with the workspaces
footer — two copies of a deliberate surrender would each have been free to
surrender differently.

### Handing the terminal to a child — `internal/ui/teaexec`

**The race (Bubble Tea v2.1.1, DEVDESK-290).** Bubble Tea's exec path is
`stopRenderer`, `ExecCommand.Run`, `startRenderer`. `stopRenderer` sends on an
unbuffered channel: it returns when the render goroutine has received the signal,
not when it has finished, and that goroutine then runs `ticker.Stop()` on its
own. `startRenderer` reuses the same ticker (`Reset`). When the child returns at
once (failed start, missing binary), `Reset` can run before the late `Stop()`:
the ticker stays stopped and the screen never repaints while the program keeps
handling input. Nothing in the `ExecCallback` can fix it, because the callback
runs after the race is decided.

**The workaround.** `settled.Run` runs the child, then sleeps for whatever remains
of `settleDelay` (50 ms since `Run` started), also when the child failed, and
returns the child's error unchanged. The old render goroutine has time to stop
the ticker before `startRenderer` resets it. The delay is in `Run`, not in the
callback, for the reason above. A child that lasts 50 ms or more pays nothing;
the worst cost is 50 ms. The delay is probabilistic, but the tests below check
it.

**The API.** `teaexec.Process(*exec.Cmd, tea.ExecCallback)` replaces
`tea.ExecProcess`; `teaexec.Command(tea.ExecCommand, tea.ExecCallback)` replaces
`tea.Exec`. Both return a `tea.Cmd`. `Process` sets a stream only when it is
nil, like Bubble Tea's own `osExecCommand`.

**The rule.** No code outside the package calls `tea.ExecProcess`, `tea.Exec` or
`tea.Suspend`. `source_guard_test.go` (`TestNoDirectTeaExecOutsideTeaexec`) scans
the repository's Go files and fails on a direct call, by file and line; its
helper is unit-tested on positive and negative cases. A comment or an unrelated
`Exec` method does not trip it.

**The tests.** `program_test.go` runs a real `tea.Program` at `GOMAXPROCS(1)`,
where the loss is deterministic. `TestARedrawFollowsAnInstantChild` (20 runs) and
`TestARedrawFollowsAChildThatFailsAtOnce` check that the view is drawn again
after the child. Trap: `tea.WithInput(nil)` makes every exec wait 500 ms before
the child starts, so the waits in those tests are generous.

**The sentinel.** `TestUpstreamTickerRaceStillExists` runs a bare `tea.Exec` and
expects the redraw to be lost. When it fails ("Bubble Tea no longer loses the
renderer ticker"), upstream fixed the race: the wrapper can be removed.
Replace `teaexec.Process` and `teaexec.Command` with the Bubble Tea calls, delete
the package and the source guard, and update this section.

### The activity-column guard (DEVDESK-142, A-16 skeleton)

`internal/app/activity_guard_test.go` keeps every view on the activity column
(Rule 125) and keeps it there. It classifies every `command.ViewType` into one of
two lists, **per table**: a view is migrated or exempt, never both and never
neither. There is no list of tables waiting for their story any more (DEVDESK-143
closed it) and no exception to shrink:

| List | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `migratedTables` | the view's tables are on the activity column (`:jobs`: `jobs/runs`, `jobs/targets`; ws: `ws`; `:sec`: `sec/inventory`; OCI: `oci/images`, `oci/networks`, `oci/volumes`, `oci/registries`, `oci/registry-browser`; explorer: `explorer/tree`, `explorer/clone-list`; templates: `templates`; netdiag: `netdiag/ports`; `:agent-usage`: `agent-usage/agents`; containers: `containers`) |
| `exemptViews` | views with no activity to show (dashboard, status, git-auth, configuration, about, files, viewer), each with its reason |

A view in neither list, or an exempt view that is also migrated, fails by name (`classificationProblems`, unit-tested on fictitious classifications). A migrated view
exposes `ActivityTables() map[string]datatable.ActivityTable` (a read-only face:
`Shapes()` and `RenderedWidth()`, see `ui-components.md`); an exempt view that reports any table fails with "remove the exception".

The netdiag view's `migratedSources` are two files only, `ports_model.go` and `ports_activity.go` (DEVDESK-150): netdiag migrates its Ports tab alone, and the guard scans the files that belong to it. `ports_commands.go` is left out: its `portsTickCmd` is the data refresh tick, not a row animation (same reasoning as OCI's `commands.go`). The other tabs (`forward_model.go`, checks, interfaces) are not migrated. It reports `netdiag/ports` from `ActivityTables()`, and its footer seed (`seedNetdiagFooter`) opens the Ports tab with one socket whose kill is in flight, driving the view's `Update` directly (no `Cmd` is run: no socket table read, no signal sent).

The `:agent-usage` view's `migratedSources` is the whole `ui/agentusageview/` package (no `tea.Tick` in it: `pollTickCmd` sleeps inside a `Cmd`), it reports `agent-usage/agents` from `ActivityTables()` and implements `WantsBlink()`; its footer seed (`seedAgentUsageFooter`) puts a transcript with a fresh line on disk and expects `indicator.Running`, without running the 2 s poll `Cmd`.

The templates view's `migratedSources` is the whole `ui/templates/` package; it reports `templates` from `ActivityTables()` and has a footer seed (a sync running on the selected row).

The explorer's `migratedSources` is the whole `explorer` package (no frame or `jobFrame` left in it). The explorer reports `explorer/clone-list` from `ActivityTables()` even with no clone running (same constructor), so the table is checked at 60 columns. The registry side adds `jobs.SafeCause` (credentials removed from a cause) and `jobs.CancelledDetail`.

**Checked at run time**, on each view built by the router: column 0 of every
migrated table is the indicator (untitled, fixed, `IconColumnWidth`, no `Less`,
no `Search`); `RenderedWidth()` equals `width-2` after a 60-column resize
(Rule 116); the help holds the `indicator.Legend` section.

**Checked by source analysis**, on migrated packages only (`ui/jobsview/`, `ui/workspaces/`, `ui/security/`): no
`AdvanceSpinner` call, no `StatusColumn:` key, no `Frame`/`frame`/`SpinnerFrame`
field or selector (`RenderedFrame` is allowed), no string or rune literal
holding an indicator glyph. Verified to fail on a positive case by injecting a `Frame`
field, an `AdvanceSpinner` call and a `"◉"` literal into `jobsview`.

6	## Le footer — `components.FooterMessage`
7	
8	One line of state below every viewport, and **one implementation**. There were
9	eight, one per view, each with its own pair of fields, its own clear message and
10	its own lipgloss block — which is precisely how the errors ended up left-aligned
11	everywhere while the notices were centred: nobody ever centred the error branch,
12	in any of the eight.
13	
14	```go
15	type Model struct { footer sharedcomponents.FooterMessage }
16	
17	// From Update() only (Rule 110). The Cmd is the expiry timer; a message set
18	// without it never clears.
19	return m, m.footer.Error("Failed to load — check logs")
20	return m, m.footer.Warn("Scan already in progress")

568	### The selected row in the footer (DEVDESK-140)
569	
570	The footer can say what the selected row is doing, in the same words the
571	activity column's state implies. Every migrated view uses it (DEVDESK-142 to
572	153); the exempt views have no row activity to say (see the guard in
573	`app-shell.md`).
574	
575	**`jobs.ActiveOn(runs, context, target, kinds...) []jobs.Active`**
576	(`internal/jobs/active.go`). The running and queued items on a target in a
577	context: running first, then queued, each group in run order. Target is
578	normalised with `TargetKey` on both sides. No `kinds` keeps every kind. Items
579	are copied without their cancel hook. No match returns nil.
580	
581	**`Status.Detail` and `RowDetail`.** `Status` gains a `Detail RowDetail`
582	(`footer_message.go`); `Status.Text` then becomes the batch progress that
583	follows it. `RowDetail{Glyph, Lead, Target, Tail}` is one sentence; `Target` is
584	a field of its own because only a path is ever shortened.
585	
586	- **`RowStatusLine(detail, progress, width)`** (`jobs_status.go`) joins
587	  them as `<detail> · <progress>` (`rowSeparator`) on at most `width` columns.
588	  Zero detail: the progress alone. No progress: the detail alone.
589	- **Cut order.** A path target shrinks first with `theme.ShortPath`, never
590	  below `minPathCols` (6), then the end of the detail is truncated. An image
591	  reference is not a path (`isPathTarget`: absolute or `~`) and is only
592	  truncated. If fewer than `minDetailCols` (8) columns are left for the detail
593	  (or fewer than it needs, when it is shorter), the detail is dropped whole and
594	  the progress stands alone.
595	- **Precedence is unchanged:** error → warning → info → status. `Detail` is
596	  part of the status, so a footer message still wins over it.
597	- **A detail with a glyph suppresses the spinner:** the row's own dot already
598	  moves.
599	- **East Asian width.** `centerLine` pads by `lipgloss.Width`, which counts
600	  ambiguous glyphs as one cell. `View` shrinks its target width by
601	  `theme.StringWidth(line) - lipgloss.Width(line)` so the line is `width`
602	  columns for `runewidth` too.
603	
604	**One constructor of sentences** (`row_activity.go`). The view fills a
605	`RowQuery{Runs, Failures, Context, Target, Kinds, Observed, ObservedText, Extra}`
606	(runs and failures of any context; they are filtered here) and calls:
607	
608	- **`RowState(q)`**: the `indicator.State` for the activity column, no text.
609	- **`DescribeRow(q)`**: `RowActivity{State, Detail}`. Both go through
610	  `resolveRow`, so the glyph in the table and the sentence in the footer cannot
611	  disagree. The state follows `indicator.Resolve` (running > queued > failure >
612	  observed > idle).
